name: john
plain: `john` (John the Ripper) guesses passwords from their hashes. A hash is a one-way scramble of a password: you cannot unscramble it, but you can scramble guesses until one matches.

It has three ways to guess: a wordlist (try every word in a file), wordlist plus rules (try Password1, p@ssword, PASSWORD...), and incremental (brute force every combination). In CTFs it is usually wordlist first, rules second.
john needs the hashes in its own input format. The helper tools zip2john, rar2john, ssh2john, pdf2john, office2john and unshadow turn files into that format.
when: Crack a hash found in a challenge (MD5, SHA, bcrypt, NTLM...).
Recover the password of an encrypted ZIP, RAR, PDF, Office file or SSH key.

examples.title: Crack a hash file with a wordlist
examples.explain: Tries every line of rockyou.txt against each hash. john guesses the hash type; if it asks, name it with --format.

examples.title: Tell john the hash type
examples.explain: Plain MD5 hashes are not auto-detected reliably. --format=raw-md5 removes the doubt. List formats with --list=formats.

examples.title: Show what was cracked
examples.explain: Cracked passwords are stored in ~/.john/john.pot. --show prints them next to their hashes without cracking again.

examples.title: Crack a ZIP password
examples.explain: zip2john extracts the part john needs into a text file, then john cracks it.

examples.title: Crack an SSH private key passphrase
examples.explain: A passphrase protects the key. ssh2john converts it, then john guesses the phrase.

examples.title: Linux passwords
examples.cmd:
unshadow passwd shadow > unshadowed.txt
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt unshadowed.txt
examples.explain: unshadow joins /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow into one file john can read.

examples.title: Add mangling rules
examples.explain: Rules mutate each word (capitalise, add 1, swap a for @), catching human habits.

examples.title: Brute-force short passwords
examples.explain: Tries every combination. Fine for 4 to 6 characters; hopeless for long passwords.

examples.title: Resume after stopping
examples.explain: john saves progress. After Ctrl+C or a crash, --restore continues where it stopped.

mistakes: Cracking the wrong format because auto-detect guessed: always check with --format and --list=formats.
Forgetting john remembers: a hash cracked earlier is only shown with --show, not recracked.
Using rockyou with rules on a slow hash (bcrypt) and expecting speed.
Running on a file that still has the converter's extra lines: only the tool's output line should be in the hash file.
try: Hash a word with echo -n password | md5sum, put the hash in a file, crack it with john and rockyou.
Make a ZIP with a simple password, crack it with zip2john and john.
List formats with john --list=formats | head and pick the one for a bcrypt hash.
see_also: hashcat(1), zip2john(1), ssh2john(1), unshadow(8), hash-identifier(1), hashid(1), and the wordlists in /usr/share/wordlists.
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
